questions.q: Why does this lesson say to always use === instead of == in JavaScript?
options: == is slower to execute than ===
== quietly converts types before comparing (so "5" == 5 is true), while === compares value and type with no conversion
== only works on numbers, never on strings
There's no actual difference — it's purely a style preference
questions.explain: Loose equality's implicit type conversion produces results that look like bugs; strict equality avoids that entirely.

questions.q: What happens in a switch statement's case block if you forget the break keyword?
options: JavaScript throws a syntax error immediately
Only the default case will ever run
The entire switch statement is skipped
Execution "falls through" and continues running the code in the next case
questions.explain: Without break, control falls through into whatever case comes next, regardless of whether it matches.

questions.q: When should you reach for a for loop instead of a while loop, according to this lesson?
options: When you know how many times you want to repeat something, like looping over a fixed range
There is no difference between for and while loops in JavaScript
for loops cannot use a counter variable
Only when looping over network requests
questions.explain: for suits a known repeat count; while suits repeating until a condition becomes false, like retrying a failed request.

questions.q: In the if/else example, if balance is 0, which branch runs?
options: Neither branch runs and the script throws an error
Both branches run one after another
The if branch, logging "Funds available"
The else branch, logging "Wallet is empty"
questions.explain: balance > 0 is false when balance is 0, so the else branch executes.

questions.q: What does null === undefined evaluate to in JavaScript?
options: false
true
"null"
It throws a TypeError
questions.explain: Strict equality considers null and undefined different types, so === returns false even though == would return true.
